lessons.title: Lesson 1: Consent comes first
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask for and record informed consent before you use anyone's story, photo or words.
This lesson builds toward: Before using anyone's story, photo or words, you will ask for and record written informed consent, including where it will be shared and how they want to be named, with the person told they can say no or change their mind without losing help.
A person's story is theirs. Before you share it, ask for informed consent: they understand what you will share, where (newsletter, website, social media, grant reports), for how long, and that they can say no or change their mind without losing any help.
Get consent in writing with a simple form, and for children get a parent or guardian's consent. Let the person choose: real name, first name only, or a changed name; photo or no photo. Write down what they agreed to and keep it with the story.
Some stories should not be told even with consent if sharing could put the person at risk, for example survivors of abuse, people in immigration cases or people in recovery. When unsure, ask your director. Your organization may have its own consent form; use it. Ask a lawyer or your umbrella association if you need a form reviewed.
Step by step:
- Explain what you will share, where and for how long.
- Make clear they can say no without losing any help.
- Let them choose name, photo and details.
- Get a signature (a parent or guardian for children).
- Keep the form with the story and respect any change of mind.
Words to know:
- Informed consent: a clear yes given by someone who understands exactly how their story will be used.
- Guardian: an adult legally responsible for a child.
Try it now: Write a five-line consent checklist for your organization covering what, where, how long, name and photo choices, and the right to say no. Compare it with any form your organization already uses.
You can now ask for and record informed consent before sharing someone's story.

check.q: Which naming choice should the person be offered?
options: Real name, first name only, or a changed name
Only a photo with no name
check.why: Let the person choose how they are named, and whether a photo is used.

check.q: A survivor of abuse wants to share her story, but sharing could put her at risk. What do you do?
options: Ask your director, because some stories should not be told even with consent
Share it with her full name
Post it only on social media
check.why: Some stories should not be told even with consent if sharing could put the person at risk.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Telling a story with dignity
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Rewrite a story so the person is the hero, not a victim.
This lesson builds toward: Given a draft story, you will rewrite it so the person is the hero, using people-first words and no pity words, leaving out details that could identify or embarrass them.
Dignity means showing people as capable people with their own strengths and choices, not as helpless victims. The person is the hero of the story; your organization is the helper.
Use people-first words ("a man experiencing homelessness", not "a homeless man"). Avoid pity words like "poor", "suffering" or "broken". Do not exaggerate. Use their own words in quotes when they agreed to it.
Leave out details that are not needed and could identify or embarrass them: exact addresses, health details, legal problems, children's school names.
Step by step:
- Make the person the main actor in the story.
- Use people-first words.
- Remove pity words and exaggeration.
- Remove details that are not needed.
- Use their own words if they agreed.
Words to know:
- Dignity: showing people with respect, as capable people with their own strengths.
- People-first language: naming the person before the situation, like "a woman experiencing homelessness".
Try it now: Rewrite this sentence with dignity: "Poor, broken Maria was homeless and helpless until we saved her." Make Maria the hero and remove pity words.
You can now write about the people you serve with dignity and respect.

check.q: In a dignity-based story, what is your organization's role?
check.why: The person is the hero; your organization is the helper.

check.q: A draft says "poor Mrs. [Name] was suffering." What do you do?
options: Remove the pity words and show her strengths and choices
check.why: Avoid pity words like "poor" and "suffering"; show people as capable.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: A simple story structure plus one honest number
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Shape a story as Before, Turning point, After, and add one true program number.
This lesson builds toward: Given story notes, you will organize the story as Before, Turning point, After and add one honest program number, with the number taken from your own checked records.
A simple structure makes a story easy to follow. Before: what life was like and what the person wanted. Turning point: what they did, with your program's help. After: what changed, in concrete terms.
Then add one honest number to show the story is part of something bigger: "Maria is one of 84 parents who finished our job training program this year." Use numbers from your own records, and do not round up or guess.
One person's story makes people care; the number shows the size of your impact. Funders want both.
Step by step:
- Write Before: life and goal.
- Write Turning point: their action with your help.
- Write After: the concrete change.
- Add one honest number from your records.
- Check the number with the person who keeps your data.
Words to know:
- Impact: the real change your work makes in people's lives.
- Outcome: a measurable result, like "84 parents finished training".
Try it now: Using a consented story or a made-up practice story, write three short lines (Before, Turning point, After) and one honest number from your program.
You can now shape a story with a clear structure and support it with a true number.

check.q: What goes in the Turning point?
options: What the person did, with your program's help
check.why: The Turning point is what they did, with your program's help.

check.q: You think about 90 people finished the program, but your records say 84. Which do you use?
check.why: Use numbers from your own records; do not round up or guess.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Drafting and sharing stories with AI

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Drafting a story with AI, safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to turn your story notes into a draft without sharing private details.
This lesson builds toward: Given your story notes, you will write an AI prompt with placeholders and general details to get a draft, with no full name, address, health details or case notes in the prompt.
AI can turn your Before, Turning point, After notes into a smooth draft in seconds. But never paste a real person's full name, address, health details or case notes into an AI tool. Many AI tools may keep what you type.
Use placeholders and general details: "Write a 150-word newsletter story. [Name], a single parent, wanted steady work. She finished our 10-week job training and now works as a medical office assistant. 84 parents finished the program this year. Warm, respectful, people-first language, no pity words."
After you get the draft, put the real details in yourself, but only the ones the person agreed to on the consent form.
Step by step:
- Start from your structured notes.
- Replace names and private details with placeholders.
- Ask for length, tone and people-first language.
- Ask for one or two changes.
- Add only the agreed real details yourself.
Words to know:
- Placeholder: a stand-in like [Name] that you replace later.
- Draft: a first version you will check and improve.
Try it now: Turn your notes from Lesson 3 into a safe prompt with placeholders and ask AI for a 150-word newsletter story. Ask for one change, then add only the agreed details.
You can now draft an impact story with AI while protecting the person's privacy.

check.q: Why keep real names and case notes out of AI tools?
options: Many AI tools may keep what you type
AI only writes in capital letters
check.why: Many AI tools may keep what you type.

check.q: The person agreed to share their first name but not their job. What do you add to the AI draft?
check.why: Add only the real details the person agreed to on the consent form.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Adapting one story for different audiences
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn one story into a newsletter piece, a social post and a grant report paragraph.
This lesson builds toward: Given one story draft, you will adapt it into a newsletter story, a social post and a grant report paragraph, using each version only where the consent form allows.
Different readers need different versions. Donors in a newsletter want warmth and a way to help. Social media needs short words and one clear action. A grant report needs facts, outcomes and how the funder's money helped.
Ask AI to adapt the draft: "Turn this story into a 40-word social post with one call to action, and a 100-word grant report paragraph that states the outcome and the number." Only use the story in places the person agreed to.
Images made by AI should never pretend to be real people you serve. If you use an AI-made image, label it, and do not use one to stand in for a real client.
Step by step:
- Check the consent form for where you may share.
- Ask AI for a short social version with one action.
- Ask AI for a grant report version with outcomes and the number.
- Compare the versions for truth.
- Label any AI-made image.
Words to know:
- Audience: the people who will read or see what you share.
- Grant report: a report to a funder showing what their money did.
Try it now: Ask AI to adapt your newsletter story into a 40-word social post and a 100-word grant report paragraph. Check that each place is allowed on the consent form.
You can now adapt one story for donors, social media and funders.

check.q: What do donors reading a newsletter want?
options: Warmth and a way to help
check.why: Newsletter donors want warmth and a way to help.

check.q: You have no photo of the real person, so AI makes a picture of a smiling family. How do you use it?
options: Say it is the family you served
Label it as AI-made and do not present it as a real client
Put the person's name under it
check.why: AI-made images must be labeled and never stand in for a real client.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking a story before it goes out
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a short checklist to catch errors, made-up details and dignity problems.
This lesson builds toward: Before a story goes out, you will check it for truth, consent, dignity and numbers and fix anything that fails, with every detail matching your notes and the consent form.
AI sometimes adds details that are not true: an extra child, a job title the person never had, a quote they never said. These can hurt the person and your organization's trust.
Before sharing, check: Truth (is every detail true and in your notes?), Consent (is every detail and place allowed?), Dignity (is the person the hero, with people-first words?), and Numbers (is the number from your records?). If you can, let the person read their story before it goes out.
Keep a copy of the final version with the consent form, and remove the story if the person asks.
Step by step:
- Truth: compare every detail with your notes; remove anything AI added.
- Consent: check each detail and each place against the form.
- Dignity: hero, people-first words, no pity.
- Numbers: confirm from your records.
- Let the person read it if you can, then file it with the consent form.
Words to know:
- Fabrication: a made-up detail presented as true.
- Checklist: a list of checks you go through every time.
Try it now: Final task: run your three versions (newsletter, social post, grant paragraph) through the four checks. Fix anything that fails and note what you changed.
You can now check impact stories for truth, consent, dignity and honest numbers before sharing.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Consent No written consent for a real story, or a detail is used that was not agreed to. Written consent, or a fully made-up practice story, with naming and places recorded. The person read their story before it went out. Structure and number Missing a story part, or the number is guessed. Before, Turning point and After, plus one number from checked records. The After part shows a concrete change in the person's own words, with permission. Safe AI prompt The prompt has a full name, address, health details or case notes. Prompt uses placeholders and general details only. Asks AI for people-first language and no pity words. Three versions A version is missing or used where consent does not allow. About 150-word newsletter, 40-word social post and 100-word grant paragraph, each where consent allows. Each version fits its readers: warmth, one action, or outcomes and funding. Final check An untrue detail, pity word or unchecked number remains. All three pass Truth, Consent, Dignity and Numbers. Lists what was fixed and keeps the final copy with the consent form. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is one of the four checks before sharing?
check.why: The four checks are Truth, Consent, Dignity and Numbers.

check.q: A family asks you to remove their story a month after it was posted. What do you do?
options: Leave it up; they signed the form
Ask them to pay to remove it
check.why: Remove the story if the person asks.
